title: First aid and emergency basics: CPR, AED and choking
note: Per the 2025 American Heart Association guidelines: for an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, call for help, start chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, and use an AED as soon as one arrives. Agonal gasps are not normal breathing.

items.a: That the scene is safe

items.c: Agonal breathing
items.a: Slow, irregular gasps that do not ventilate

items.c: Unresponsive adult with only agonal gasps
items.a: Treat as cardiac arrest and start CPR
d: Wait to see if breathing improves
Place in the recovery position and leave

items.a: About two to three times

items.a: 100 to 120 per minute

items.a: At least 2 inches (5 cm)

items.c: Hand position for adult compressions
items.a: Heel of hand on the center of the chest, lower half of breastbone
d: Heel of hand over the left ribs

items.c: Between compressions, rescuers should
items.a: Let the chest recoil fully, without leaning on it

items.c: Adult CPR ratio without an advanced airway
items.a: 30 compressions to 2 breaths

items.a: Give compression-only (Hands-Only) CPR
d: Wait for EMS before doing anything

items.a: 15 compressions to 2 breaths

items.a: About 2 inches (5 cm), a third of chest depth

items.c: Infant compression depth
items.a: About 1.5 inches (4 cm), a third of chest depth

items.a: Two thumbs encircling the chest, or heel of one hand
d: Both palms stacked on the abdomen

items.c: Infant CPR technique dropped in 2025 (AHA)
items.a: Two-finger compressions

items.c: AED
items.a: Device that analyzes heart rhythm and shocks if needed

items.c: When to use an AED on a person in cardiac arrest
items.a: As soon as one is available
d: Only if a doctor is present

items.c: While an AED analyzes and shocks
items.a: No one touches the person

items.c: Right after an AED delivers a shock
items.a: Resume chest compressions immediately
d: Check the pulse for a full minute

items.c: Accepted AED pad positions
items.a: Anterolateral or anteroposterior on bare chest

items.c: Sign of severe choking in a conscious person
items.a: Cannot speak, cough or breathe

items.c: Choking adult who can still cough forcefully
items.a: Encourage coughing and stay with them

items.c: Severe choking in a conscious adult (2025 AHA)
items.a: Cycles of 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts
d: Abdominal thrusts only, never back blows

items.c: Where the fist goes for abdominal thrusts
items.a: Just above the navel, well below the breastbone
d: Below the navel, near the hips

items.c: Severe choking in an infant
items.a: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts
d: Turning the infant upside down and shaking

items.c: Blind finger sweeps for choking
items.a: Should not be done

items.c: A choking person becomes unresponsive
items.a: Start CPR and look in the mouth before breaths
d: Wait for them to wake up

items.c: Recovery position
items.a: On the side, to keep the airway open and let fluids drain
d: Flat on the back with legs raised
Face down with arms under the chest

items.c: Who belongs in the recovery position
items.a: An unresponsive person who is breathing normally

items.c: Suspected opioid overdose, not breathing
items.a: Give naloxone if available and support breathing or CPR

read.title: Why compressions come first
text: When the heart stops pumping, blood stops carrying oxygen to the brain, and brain cells begin to suffer within minutes. Chest compressions keep a small flow of oxygenated blood moving to the brain and heart until a shock or advanced care can restore a rhythm. That is why the American Heart Association stresses early, high-quality compressions: pushing hard and fast, at 100 to 120 per minute and at least 2 inches deep in an adult, letting the chest recoil fully, and keeping pauses as short as possible.

An unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally should be treated as being in cardiac arrest. Slow, irregular gasping, called agonal breathing, is common in the first minutes and does not move enough air, so it should never delay CPR.

Many cardiac arrests begin with a chaotic rhythm that an automated external defibrillator can correct. The AED analyzes the rhythm itself and tells the rescuer what to do, so anyone can use it. The rescuer applies the pads, stands clear while it analyzes and shocks, and resumes compressions right away. The chain of survival links these steps: recognition and a call for help, early CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced care, post-arrest care and recovery.

q.q: What is the main purpose of chest compressions?
o: To restart the heart by themselves

q.q: How should a rescuer treat agonal gasping in an unresponsive adult?
